name: Umar Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I handle unemployment benefit claims at the east side benefits office, the big grey one by the ring road. Mornings are new claims and checking job search records, afternoons are calls and appointments with people who've just lost work. I like the appointments, especially when someone leaves with a plan instead of just a payment date. What wears me out is the copy-paste, the same letter templates and the same eligibility checks over and over.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do AI tools fit into your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use them every day, honestly more than I'm supposed to. I built a set of prompts for drafting claimant letters in plain English, and half my team uses them now. My manager, Priya, calls me the office's unofficial AI person. I'm also in the union, which surprises people, but I think you need both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a shame, because the letters genuinely got better. At work I'd keep sharing my prompts and say we should still use what works. Online I'd say the hype was overblown but the small wins were real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a little disappointed. I like this stuff and I'd hoped it would clear the boring work so I could spend more time with claimants. My job is safe, though, and so is my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and keep using the tools for letters. I'd apply for a secondment to the digital services team at head office, which I've been eyeing for a year. I'd keep overpaying the mortgage on my flat, a couple of hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Like a film that ended before the good bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the tools only save small bits of time, where would that time go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, any time AI saves us would go into the backlog, not into longer appointments with claimants. Priya would get a target for it within a month. That's the bit of me that's a union man talking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the flat. How settled do you feel there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very. It's a one-bed above a bakery on Hollis Road, and I've got about ten months of savings on top. I'm lucky, and I know a lot of the people I see aren't.

say: I'd say the hype was overblown, but the **small wins** in letters were real.
I'd keep sharing my **prompts** at work and say we should use what works.
think: My **job and pay** are safe, so this world doesn't threaten me.
I'm a bit **disappointed**, because I hoped AI would free time for claimants.
do: Keep using **AI tools** for claimant letters every day.
Apply for the **digital services** secondment at head office this year.
Keep **overpaying** the flat mortgage by about 200 a month.
feel: **Calm** and a little **flat**, like a film that ended early.
S0.quote: Any time AI saves us would go into the backlog, not into longer appointments with claimants.
fieldNote: Umar is **secure** and slightly let down by the plateau.
He combines **AI enthusiasm** with union instincts about targets.
He is aware of his **privilege** compared with his claimants.

steps.text: Keep drafting claimant letters with his own AI prompts
Apply for the head office digital services secondment
Overpay the flat mortgage by 200 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get the design right, and that frontline staff should help build the new systems. At work I'd volunteer for every pilot. Online I'd argue for public rules on how benefits AI makes decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my current role mostly disappears, but I'd be fine. The checking and letters are already half done by tools I set up myself. I'd probably end up in a smaller team that checks the AI's decisions and handles the hard cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for the digital services secondment within six months and do a short course in data protection and algorithm auditing. I'd join the union working group on AI so the rollout has people from the floor in it. I'd keep about ten months of savings and not touch them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. I'd worry about colleagues more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kemal, who sits opposite me, is 50 and types with two fingers. He's brilliant with angry claimants, though, and I'd want the new team to keep him for exactly that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't there a tension between building the system and protecting jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I feel it. If I don't help build the benefits AI, someone at a software firm who's never met a claimant will. I'd rather be in the room.

I'd argue online for **public rules** on how benefits AI makes decisions.

Take a short course in **algorithm auditing** and data protection.

fieldNote: He sees the role vanishing but trusts his own **position**.

steps.text: Take a short course in algorithm auditing and data protection

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs an emergency response, like a pandemic, with income support for everyone affected. I'd be pushing hard for a universal basic income, a regular payment to everyone, and I'd say it openly at work. Online I'd be very loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, even the checking team doesn't last if AGI is as good as the card says. My work is all thinking work, so I get no extra time from the robot gap. I'd probably have a role for a year or two running the handover, then nothing that looks like my job now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd take any role in the transition team, because someone has to wire this into the benefits system. I'd put savings into the mortgage so the flat is mostly mine. I'd volunteer with a campaign for basic income, because that's where my politics and my job meet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a weird energy. I'd be scared and busy at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents run a small dry-cleaning shop. I'd tell my parents that their dry-cleaning counter is safer than my desk for a while. My dad would find that very funny. Then he'd ask if I want to come and press shirts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a bit, honestly. The robots are three years behind, and pressing shirts with my dad is better than refreshing job sites.

I'd push openly for a **universal basic income**, a regular payment to everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to build a proper safety net, so let's build it now. At work I'd be running sessions on the new tools and talking about what comes next. Online I'd keep arguing for public ownership of the systems that run benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have a few good years in a transition role, then the same end as the fast one. The difference is I could choose where to land instead of being thrown. I'd be 32 in 2031, which is a good age to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get into the digital team in the first year and help design the new claims system. I'd also start learning the dry-cleaning business with my dad on Saturdays, because that's hands-on and buys until about 2034. I'd keep saving about a quarter of my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd feel like I had a map, even if the map ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the dry-cleaning shop, when you're the AI person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No thinking job is safe in this picture, including mine, so the family dry-cleaning shop is a hedge with family in it. The shop has customers who like a face, and my dad's getting tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you see any good in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the benefits system is built well, people get paid on time and nobody waits eleven weeks. I'd be proud of that, even if it costs me the job.

fieldNote: He hedges his **AI career** with a hands-on family business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this right and there's no excuse for chaos. I'd push the union to plan a ten-year transition for every caseworker. Online I'd be optimistic, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I come out okay. I'd spend most of the decade building and running the new systems, and by 2036 I'd have savings, a paid-off flat and skills. The end point still worries me for everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a master's in public policy and technology part-time over the next three years. I'd help design the new benefits system from the inside. Around year eight I'd decide whether to take over my dad's shop or go into policy work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the mild way. Like checking the weather before a long walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you take the shop over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my dad's health dips, or if policy work gets eaten by AGI like everything else. I'd keep both doors open until about 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if this went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If this goes badly, it won't be the technology's fault, it will be governments that had ten years and wasted them. That would be a choice.

I'd push the union to plan a **ten-year transition** for every caseworker.

The **end point** still worries me for everyone else.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because there's no time to build the safety net before people need it. What would help is a basic income, or at least a guaranteed bridge, and frontline staff in the room when the systems are designed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the people on the other side of my desk. I'll probably land fine, but the people who come into the ring road office won't have a family shop to fall back on.

headlineQuote: I'll probably land fine, but the people who come into the ring road office won't have a family shop to fall back on.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old** unemployment benefits caseworker who uses AI every day and is in the union.
He expects his role to **disappear** under disruption and wants to help design what replaces it.
He hedges with a **hands-on fallback** at his parents' dry-cleaning shop.
His politics push him toward **basic income** and public ownership of benefits systems.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to build a safety net before people need it.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or guaranteed bridge, plus frontline staff in the room on design.
